checks.prompt: The highlighted cell is a Nash equilibrium. Which reason is correct?

options.text: Neither player can gain by switching their own move alone, given the other player's move.
options.why: That is the definition: an equilibrium is stable, and it does not have to be the best outcome for either player.

options.text: Both players get the highest payoff available in the whole matrix.
options.why: An equilibrium is only a stable cell. Another cell can pay both players more, so stability is not the same as being the best outcome.

options.text: Both players are certain to choose it, so it is what they will do.
options.why: An equilibrium describes stability, not a prediction. Players may miss it or play another cell.

options.text: Each player's move is a dominant strategy, so the other player's choice does not matter.
options.why: An equilibrium only needs each move to be a best response to the other's move. That is weaker than dominance.

checks.prompt: This game is a Prisoner's dilemma. Which feature makes it one?

options.text: Defecting is a dominant strategy for each player, and mutual cooperation gives both players a higher payoff than mutual defection.
options.why: Dominance makes defection each player's move, and mutual cooperation is still better for both, so the equilibrium is Pareto-dominated.

options.text: Both players are selfish and only want more money, so each defects.
options.why: Payoffs measure what each player cares about, not money, and the game does not assume selfishness. The feature that defines the game is dominance.

options.text: Mutual defection is the worst outcome for both players, so the game is a Chicken game.
options.why: In Chicken, mutual defection is the worst outcome and there is no dominant strategy. This game has a dominant strategy, which is what separates it.

options.text: Each player has a dominant strategy to cooperate, so the outcome is good for both.
options.why: Cooperation is not dominant here, and even a dominant strategy does not make the outcome good.

checks.prompt: The stepper removes only strictly dominated strategies. Why does the order of its removals not change the set that survives?

options.text: Removing other strategies cannot rescue a strictly dominated one, so every order removes the same strategies.
options.why: A strategy that loses to another strategy keeps losing after other strategies are removed, so the order does not change the result.

options.text: Weakly dominated strategies can be removed in any order, because removing them never removes an equilibrium.
options.why: Weak elimination is order-dependent and can remove equilibria. The stepper is strict and pure-strategy only for this reason.

options.text: Any row can be removed, because every row is dominated by some other row.
options.why: A strategy can be removed only if another strategy is strictly better against every remaining move. Not every row is dominated.

checks.prompt: Tit for tat ranks near the top of this round robin. Why could a different population or noise level change the ranking?

options.text: The ranking is relative to the other strategies, and noise changes the moves they see, so the result belongs to this tournament.
options.why: Tit for tat's rank depends on the field and on the played moves. Axelrod's results are specific to his tournaments, and this app computes its own ranking live.

options.text: Tit for tat wins every tournament, so its rank cannot change.
options.why: No single tournament makes this a general rule. Tit for tat did well in Axelrod's tournaments, but a different population or noise level can change the order.

options.text: Noise does not matter, because tit for tat copies the opponent's last move exactly.
options.why: Noise flips played moves, and tit for tat responds to played moves, so noise changes the sequence of play.

checks.prompt: The players in the reveal are labelled 'Simulated players (a model, not real people)'. What does the level histogram show?

options.text: The level counts follow the mix assumed in the model, so they show the model's assumptions, not measurements of real people.
options.why: The players are generated from assumed level mixes. The histogram follows from those assumptions and is not data about a crowd.

options.text: The level counts are what a real crowd of people guessed in a survey.
options.why: This game has no real crowd. Real figures appear only with a source link, and this histogram is not one of them.

options.text: 0 is the equilibrium, so the histogram shows that the crowd will guess 0.
options.why: 0 is the equilibrium, which is a stability property, not a forecast of what anyone guesses. The reveal says 0 is not the winning guess.

checks.prompt: In a second-price auction with private values, why is bidding your value a dominant strategy?

options.text: Your bid decides whether you win, but not the price you pay, so no other bid does better than bidding your value.
options.why: Bidding your value wins exactly when winning pays less than your value, and loses when winning would cost more. Any other bid can do worse, never better.

options.text: The price is the second bid, so the winner pays less and the outcome is good for everyone.
options.why: Truthful bidding is dominant, but dominance does not imply a good outcome for the seller or for everyone.

options.text: The second bid sets the price, so every bidder gains by bidding as high as possible.
options.why: Bidding as high as possible can win at a price above your value, so it is not dominant.

checks.prompt: In a common-value auction with noisy estimates, why does the winning bidder often overpay?

options.text: The winner is likely the bidder whose estimate was most too high, so in this setup the winning bid tends to exceed the true value.
options.why: With one common value and independent noisy estimates, the highest estimate is the most likely to be an overestimate. In this setup, bidders who ignore that lose on average.

options.text: Winners always overpay in every auction, whatever the format or information.
options.why: The result is specific to this setup, with a common value and uniform noise. It is not a fact about all auctions.

options.text: The winner is always the bidder who values the item most.
options.why: In a common-value auction everyone is estimating the same value from noisy signals. The highest estimate need not be the most accurate one.
